To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of intradermaly injected mature dendritic cells do not migrate to the draining node but remain at the site where they were injected and that they attract and activate antigen-specific T cells.

(i) intradermally inoculated mature dendritic cells are not only able to induce an immune response, but also to attract antigen-specific T cells; (ii) this immune response is not only directed against the antigen presented by the dendritic cells but also against the antigen presented at other sites; and (iii) dendritic cells are able to induce an effective immune response in the absence of lymph node migration.
dendritic cells injected into skin remain at the site and attract T cells, which specifically recognize peptide epitope presented by the injected cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cellular and molecular interactions of dendritic cells, T cells, and endothelial cells during the initiation of an immune response.
the analysis of dendritic cells in the context of the immune response to tumors.
the cellular and molecular interactions between dendritic cells and T cells in the context of therapeutic dendritic cell vaccines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of the injected cells do not migrate, but that the cells that remain at the site do not act as "decoy" cells.

the injected dendritic cell vaccine induces an immune response that is initiated in the draining lymph nodes and that the immune response is then maintained by an ongoing antigenic stimulus in the tumor microenvironment.
dendritic cell vaccination is a complex immunological event, which is not yet well understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the injected dendritic cell vaccine is able to attract naive and central memory CD8(+) T cells to the site of inoculated dendritic cells and induce specific T cell activation and proliferation.

the injection site of dendritic cells can be considered an "immunologic organ", in which the injected antigen-specific T cells are retained by a specific interaction with the antigen-presenting dendritic cells and where the dendritic cell-primed T cells are activated by dendritic cell-produced cytokines and by the dendritic cell-presented peptide epitope.
dendritic cells, which do not migrate to the draining LN after therapeutic vaccination, nevertheless are able to attract antigen specific T cells to the site of inoculations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of intradermaly injected dendritic cells remain at the inoculation sight and that these dendritic cells are able to attract and activate naive and memory T cells.
dendritic cells injected intradermally are not only able to induce an immune response in the lymph nodes but also to induce a local immune response.
dendritic cells injected into skin tissue induce a specific, antigen-dependent immune response, even if the cells fail to migrate to the draining secondary lymphatic organ.
